text: Body condition: skinny condition can signal feed deficiency, chronic disease, or parasite infestation, and skinny cattle recover more slowly; conversely, a sick animal that is still in good body condition should raise suspicion of an acute disease. Skin: rough hair, discoloration, and crusts often reflect vitamin/mineral deficiency and leave the animal weaker against infection; photosensitization is common in Cambodia and fairly easy to identify. Movement: observe the standing animal first for weakness (e.g. post-calving deficiency) or incoordination (e.g. from nervous diseases like botulism); while walking, lameness shows as paddling from foot to foot, a tendency to lie down after a few minutes, or refusal to bear weight on one leg. Breathing: normal rate is 10–20/minute in adults with thorax and abdomen moving together; high temperature or respiratory disease clearly raises the rate and can cause open-mouth breathing; coughing is easier to detect when the animal is moving. Feces: color ranges from black to greenish depending on diet and liver function; blood or mucus can indicate Liver Fluke; diarrhea can come from too much young grass or from parasites; constipation can occur when cattle eat too little due to high temperatures.
